items.abstract: <jats:p>The aim of the work was to determine how much consumers are aware of the benefits of whole grain products, and whether and how this awareness affects their buying habits. Primary data were collected through a survey questionnaire (non-random sample), then processed in Excel and presented graphically. The results show that the majority of respondents are aware of the benefits of whole grain products and that this awareness greatly influences their purchasing habits. In addition, consumers are influenced by lifestyle, product taste, health benefits, tasting, advertising, price and other people's opinion about the product, etc. Those who answered that they do not consume whole grain products cited the high price as the main reason. They have received information about the benefits of whole grain products from family, relatives, friends, acquaintances, Internet experts and colleagues, but they still lack information. Also, promotion largely creates consumer awareness. Price reduction, tasting, improved taste and promotion would contribute to greater realization of whole grain products. Creating educational campaigns about the benefits of whole grain products would encourage consumers to buy more of them, which would increase their production and have a positive impact on public health.</jats:p>
title: Consumer Awareness of the Benefits of Whole Grain Products and Influence on Purchasing Habits

items.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: This paper establishes a novel theoretical framework (Individual Habit-Based Consumer Theory) to reframe automatic habits as distinct economic goods, formalizing habit loop mechanics within rational choice theory to explain persistent, seemingly irrational human behaviors. Design/methodology/approach: The study develops an axiomatic microeconomic optimization model. Habits are treated as endogenous goods with non monetary prices derived from automaticity, inconsistency, and cue frequency, optimized under a constrained behavioral resource budget. Findings: Cumulative repetition endogenously lowers a habit’s behavioral price, creating a lock-in effect. This frames the intention-behavior gap as an economic optimization under high initial switching costs rather than psychological failure. Research limitations/implications: As a pure theoretical framework, this research lacks empirical validation. Future paradigms must experimentally test the proposed hypotheses using neuroimaging or automated behavioral tracking data collected via wearable technologies. Practical implications: Motivational interventions are inefficient if a behavior's initial resource barrier is too high. Practitioners should prioritize environmental choice architecture that systematically lowers the dynamic price of desirable habits through task simplification. Social implications: Policymakers can leverage this framework to scale public health and environmental campaigns. Shifting from information dissemination to structural cue design optimizes population welfare under limited cognitive or temporal resource constraints. Originality/value: This paper is the first to mathematically formalize the psychological habit loop within individual consumer theory. It uniquely redefines behavioral inertia as a structural problem of resource allocation under dynamic pricing.</jats:p>
title: Reframing "Habits" As Distinct "Economic Goods": A Novel "Individual Habit-Based Consumer Theory"
